paper.title: Automatic arrangement of music into notated scores for chosen instruments: a systematic web search of software, services and research systems (November 2026)

not_claimed.why: tally.py and agreement.py compared the coding pass with integers while the record stores it as text, so PL2's runs RN3 and RN4 counted no coding and computed no agreement; their zeros say nothing about the systems. PL3 repeated the same estimands on the same codings with the scripts fixed; its analysis text says the same steps in other words. tally.py kept only codings whose pass equals the integer 1, but the record stores pass as the string '1', so it counted no coding: every count in RN3 is 0. agreement.py compared pass with the integers 1 and 2, but the record stores pass as strings, so it found no dossier coded by both coders and computed no agreement. The repeat words the analysis differently, as the person who confirmed the void read: PL2 planned "Run 1: claimset-code/score-arrangers-2026/tally.py counts pass-1 systems: in total; with each code; by method and availability; by platform and method; by pricing and method; and, among systems with notated output for a user-chosen instrumentation, by input (score or other) and method; it also counts systems without exactly one method or availability code, as a check. Run 2: claimset-code/score-arrangers-2026/agreement.py gives, per code, Krippendorff's alpha (two coders, nominal) and the share of dossiers agreed, over the dossiers both coders coded."; PL3 planned "Run 1: claimset-code/score-arrangers-2026/tally.py (fixed) counts pass-1 systems: total; with each code; by method and availability; by platform and method; by pricing and method; among notated chosen-instrument systems by input and method; and systems without exactly one method or availability code. Run 2: agreement.py (fixed) gives per code Krippendorff's alpha (two coders, nominal) and share of dossiers agreed over the dossiers both coders coded.".
not_claimed.statement: PL2's planned counts and coder agreement for the 36 systems: void, a script bug gave zeros; repeated by PL3 (C2).

protocol.question: As of November 2026, which software products, online services and research systems can automatically or semi-automatically arrange existing music into a notated score that musicians read, for a set of instruments the user chooses; and for each, what input it takes, what notation it outputs, whether it uses machine learning or rules, and whether it works interactively or in real time?
sources: WebSearch (Claude's web search tool, standard mode)
include: An arranging system (TM1): software product, online service or research system that automatically or semi-automatically produces instrumental parts from existing musical material
Arranges for more than one instrument, or offers a choice of instrument, or produces notation (so the codebook can apply)
Public information about it is available at retrieval (product page, documentation, paper or forum account)
exclude: Human arranging services (people hired to arrange)
Audio-only generators that output finished audio with no parts (e.g. text-to-song)
Pure transcription (audio to notation of the same parts) with no arranging
Notation editors and DAWs without an arranging function
Generators of a single line only (melody, chord progression or drum loop) with no arrangement across instruments
Pages that name no system (general articles), except roundups and threads, which are used for snowballing

declarations.competing_interests: The guarantor, Ivan Svetunkov, founded Syntonic Labs, which develops Tempered Arranger, a machine-learning arranging product in the market this study scans; Syntonic Labs products were excluded from the scan.

paper.summary: We searched the web in November 2026 for software and research systems that turn existing music into written-out parts for instruments a musician chooses, and classified the 36 we found. Most commercial tools do this with fixed rules, inside notation programs like Sibelius and Dorico or as live accompaniment keyboards and plugins, while almost all research systems use machine learning. Only one commercial product, Scorehand, a chat-based plugin for MuseScore, reads a notated score, uses machine learning, writes notation and lets the user say which instruments to write for. The study was planned in advance, and its hypothesis that no such product existed was refuted.

definitions.definition: A software product, online service or research system that, from existing musical material (a melody, chords, a score or a performance), automatically or semi-automatically produces parts for instruments: by orchestrating, harmonising, voicing, exploding or reducing. The unit of analysis: one system, counted once across versions and editions.

The system delivers its arrangement as notation a musician reads: a score or parts in standard staff notation, exported as MusicXML, PDF or a notation application's file, or written into a notation editor.

code.include: The system's own description or documentation shows the arrangement as staff notation, or exports MusicXML, PDF score/parts, or a notation-app file.
code.exclude: Output only as audio, MIDI without notation, tablature or chord charts alone, or piano-roll.

definitions.definition: The user selects the instruments or ensemble the arrangement is written for.

code.include: The user picks target instruments, an ensemble, or a template of instruments, and the parts are written for that choice.
code.exclude: A fixed instrumentation (e.g. piano only, or a style's fixed band) the user cannot change instrument by instrument.

definitions.definition: The system accepts notated music as its input.

code.include: Accepts MusicXML, or works on a score inside a notation application (which reads MusicXML).
code.exclude: Accepts only audio, MIDI, chord symbols, text prompts or live playing.

definitions.definition: The arrangement is produced by a model trained on data (machine learning, neural network, LLM).

code.include: The developer states that a trained model (machine learning, neural network, deep learning, LLM, 'AI model') generates the arrangement.
code.exclude: 'AI' used as a label without saying that a trained model produces the arrangement; such systems are coded unclear method.

definitions.definition: The arrangement is produced by hand-written rules, styles, templates or algorithms without a trained model.

code.include: The developer describes style files, templates, rules, voice-leading algorithms or search procedures, or an independent review does.
code.exclude: Any trained model generating the arrangement.

definitions.definition: The sources do not say whether a trained model or rules produce the arrangement.

code.include: Marketed as 'AI' or 'intelligent' with no statement of how the arrangement is produced.
code.exclude: Either ML method or rules method applies.

definitions.definition: The arrangement is regenerated in response to the user's choices or playing without an offline export-import cycle.

code.include: Arrangement updates live as the user plays, changes instruments or settings, within the same session.
code.exclude: A one-off batch generation the user must re-run from scratch.

definitions.definition: Sold or licensed to the public (paid, subscription or freemium) at the date of retrieval.

code.include: A price, subscription or purchase page exists at retrieval.
code.exclude: Free open-source, free-only, discontinued, or research-only systems.

definitions.definition: Available to the public at no cost at retrieval.

code.include: Free download or free web use, or published code.
code.exclude: Paid-only or research descriptions without public access.

definitions.definition: Described in a research publication (paper, preprint, thesis) rather than offered as a product.

code.include: The source is a paper, preprint or thesis describing the system.
code.exclude: A product whose maker also published a paper is coded by its availability as a product.

definitions.definition: A commercially available arranging system, not made by Syntonic Labs, that takes score input and uses an ML method to produce notated output for a user-chosen instrumentation.

code.include: The same system is coded commercially available, score input, ML method, notated output and user-chosen instrumentation.
code.exclude: Any of the five missing, or the system is a Syntonic Labs product (Tempered).

definitions.definition: A fixed set of web searches run on one or two days, each result screened against the inclusion criteria, with one level of snowballing from included roundups, then each included system coded by a fixed codebook (summative content analysis, deductive).
Sold for a single payment (a perpetual licence), possibly with paid upgrades.

code.include: A one-off price or perpetual licence is listed at retrieval.
code.exclude: Subscription-only or free.

definitions.definition: Paid by recurring fee (monthly or yearly), or by credits bought repeatedly.

code.include: A monthly or yearly price, or credit packs, listed at retrieval.
code.exclude: One-off purchase only, or free.

definitions.definition: A free version or free use exists alongside paid options (freemium), or the system is wholly free.

code.include: Free plan, free version, free trial longer than a demo, or wholly free use.
code.exclude: Time-limited trial of a paid product only, or no public access.

definitions.definition: No price could be found in the dossier.

code.include: The dossier shows no price or pricing model.
code.exclude: Any price or pricing model stated.

definitions.definition: Runs as a standalone application on a computer.

code.include: Downloadable standalone program for Windows, macOS or Linux.
code.exclude: Runs only inside another host (plugin) or in a browser.

definitions.definition: Used in a web browser or through an online API.

code.include: Browser-based app or online API.
code.exclude: Desktop-only or plugin-only.

definitions.definition: Runs inside a digital audio workstation (VST, AU, AAX, MIDI effect).

code.include: Offered in a DAW plugin format.
code.exclude: Notation-app plugins; standalone apps only.

definitions.definition: Runs inside a notation application (Sibelius, Dorico, MuseScore, Finale) as a plugin or built-in feature.

code.include: A notation application's own feature, or a plugin for one.
code.exclude: Exports to a notation app without running inside it.

definitions.definition: Runs as an app on a phone or tablet.

code.include: iOS, iPadOS or Android app.
code.exclude: Mobile web only (coded web service).

definitions.definition: Available only as source code, a library or model weights, with no packaged application.

code.include: Published code, library or weights only.
code.exclude: Any packaged application, plugin or web service.

claims.statement: Among the 36 [[D1:arranging system]]s found by a [[D13:market scan]] of 20 fixed web queries with one level of snowballing (19 November 2026), one [[D9:commercially available]] system not made by Syntonic Labs, the MuseScore plugin AiHud Notation Copilot (renamed Scorehand), is a [[D12:full-match arranger]]: it takes [[D4:score input]] (the open score, sent as MusicXML), uses an [[D5:ML method]] (a server-side AI model) and writes [[D2:notated output]] for a section the user names ([[D3:user-chosen instrumentation]]); so the planned hypothesis that no such commercial system exists was not supported.

evidence.description: Lab runs RN2 under plan PL1. Design: Market scan (D13): run the 20 fixed queries in claimset-code/score-arrangers-2026/queries.txt once each (WebSearch, standard mode; 15 general and research queries, 5 aimed at Reddit, KVR, MuseScore and Gearspace forums), screen every result against the inclusion criteria, snowball one level from included roundups and forum threads, build one dossier per included system from its own pages (product page, pricing page, documentation, paper), capture it, and code it with the codebook D2-D12 and D14-D23 (pass 1, this agent). A second agent, registered before it starts and working in its own log, independently codes (pass 2) a 25% random sample of the dossiers (Python random.sample, seed 2026, over dossier IDs in capture order). Syntonic Labs products and human arranging services are excluded. Analysis: Count pass-1 dossiers coded full-match arranger (D12), and dossiers coded all five of commercially available, score input, ML method, notated output and user-chosen instrumentation; the two counts check each other. The verdict is computed by the tool's count over pass 1.

execution.notes: Counted by the counter of the lab record tool (claimset 0.44.6, claimset/lab/count.py) from the codings in force, recorded with the run (codings.json); the code version is the study's code checkout, not the counter's.

limitations.statement: Lab plan PL2 was made void (DC3): a defect made its runs (RN3, RN4) meaningless. DV1: tally.py kept only codings whose pass equals the integer 1, but the record stores pass as the string '1', so it counted no coding: every count in RN3 is 0. DV2: agreement.py compared pass with the integers 1 and 2, but the record stores pass as strings, so it found no dossier coded by both coders and computed no agreement. This claim is from plan PL3, which repeats it with the same analysis, reworded (both texts are in the exploration summary), and decision rule on the same data. PL3 was planned after the void runs and before its own, so what the void runs showed could have shaped it. The void runs returned only zeros for every count and no agreement values; no coding or count of any system was visible in them, so they showed nothing that could have shaped PL3 beyond the bug itself. The dossiers were coded after PL2 was planned and before PL3 was; the codebook, the codings and the analysis are those PL2 fixed, unchanged in PL3.

The scan covers only systems that 20 fixed web queries (and one level of snowballing) returned on 19 November 2026; products seen in an earlier ad-hoc search but not returned (Orb Composer, LANDR Composer, InstaComposer, Muse, RapidComposer, Texturium) are not in the counts, and a negative or positive count holds for this frame only.

Dossiers were built from WebFetch renderings of each page by a language model and from search snippets, not from byte copies of the pages; a feature a page states could be missed or misrendered, and several dossiers (Dorico, Chord Dock, Finale, research papers) rest on snippets or summaries.
